name: STM32L431CCT6
title: STM32L431xx ultra-low-power Arm Cortex-M4 microcontrollers with FPU: 80 MHz, 128 or 256 Kbytes Flash, 64 Kbytes SRAM, 1.71 V to 3.6 V
summary: An ultra-low-power 32-bit microcontroller line built on an 80 MHz Arm Cortex-M4 core with a single-precision FPU, DSP instructions and an MPU, with 128 or 256 Kbytes of single-bank ECC Flash and 64 Kbytes of SRAM (16 Kbytes of it parity-checked and kept in Standby). It runs from 1.71 V to 3.6 V with seven low-power modes reaching 8 nA in Shutdown, and carries a 5 Msps 12-bit ADC, two DAC channels, an op amp, two comparators, a voltage reference buffer, touch sensing, and CAN, SAI, Quad SPI, three I2C, three USART, an LPUART and three SPI. The family comes in nine packages from 32 to 100 pins; the STM32L431CCT6 is the 256-Kbyte part in LQFP48 for -40 to 85 °C.
key_figures: Arm Cortex-M4 with FPU, MPU, DSP; up to 80 MHz
64 Kbytes: 48 Kbytes SRAM1 + 16 Kbytes SRAM2 with parity
up to 83 fast I/Os, most 5 V tolerant; 38 on LQFP48

operation.text: Supply 1.71 V to 3.6 V; ambient -40 °C to 85, 105 or 125 °C. Low-power figures: 200 nA in VBAT mode (RTC plus 32 x 32-bit backup registers), 8 nA in Shutdown and 28 nA in Standby (each with 5 wakeup pins), 280 nA in Standby with RTC, 1.0 µA in Stop 2 (1.28 µA with RTC), 84 µA/MHz in Run, 4 µs wakeup from Stop, batch acquisition mode (BAM), brown-out reset and an interconnect matrix. Core: Arm Cortex-M4 with FPU and MPU at up to 80 MHz, 100 DMIPS, DSP instructions, ART Accelerator for 0-wait-state execution from Flash. Benchmarks: 1.25 DMIPS/MHz (Dhrystone 2.1), 273.55 CoreMark (3.42 CoreMark/MHz at 80 MHz), ULPBench score 176.7.

Clock sources: 4 to 48 MHz crystal oscillator, 32 kHz crystal oscillator for the RTC (LSE), internal 16 MHz RC trimmed in the factory to ±1%, internal low-power 32 kHz RC (±5%), internal multispeed 100 kHz to 48 MHz oscillator that the LSE can trim to better than ±0.25%, internal 48 MHz RC with clock recovery, and two PLLs for the system clock, audio and ADC. Memories: up to 256 Kbytes of single-bank Flash with proprietary code readout protection, 64 Kbytes of SRAM of which 16 Kbytes have hardware parity, and a Quad SPI memory interface.

Up to 83 fast I/Os, most of them 5 V tolerant. RTC with hardware calendar, alarms and calibration. Up to 21 capacitive sensing channels for touchkeys and linear or rotary touch sensors. Eleven timers: one 16-bit advanced motor-control, one 32-bit and two 16-bit general-purpose, two 16-bit basic, two 16-bit low-power timers that run in Stop mode, two watchdogs and SysTick. Analog with its own supply: one 12-bit 5 Msps ADC (up to 16 bits with hardware oversampling, 200 µA/Msps), two 12-bit DAC outputs with low-power sample and hold, one op amp with built-in PGA, two ultra-low-power comparators. Sixteen communication interfaces: one SAI, three I2C FM+ (1 Mbit/s) with SMBus/PMBus, four USARTs (ISO 7816, LIN, IrDA, modem), one LPUART that wakes from Stop 2, three SPIs plus one Quad SPI, CAN 2.0B active, SDMMC, SWPMI single wire protocol master, and an infrared interface. Also a 14-channel DMA, a true random number generator, a CRC unit, a 96-bit unique ID, and debug over SWD, JTAG and the Embedded Trace Macrocell. All packages are ECOPACK2.

The core is a 32-bit Arm Cortex-M4 RISC at up to 80 MHz with a single-precision FPU covering all Arm single-precision instructions and data types, the full DSP instruction set and a memory protection unit. Memories and peripherals connect through a 32-bit multi-AHB bus matrix, with two AHB and two APB buses. Flash and SRAM protection: RDP, WRP, PCROP and the firewall. Timers on chip: a 32-bit general-purpose one, a 16-bit motor-control PWM one, four 16-bit general-purpose ones and a pair of 16-bit low-power ones. The analog blocks (ADC, DAC, op amp, comparators) take their own supply input, and VBAT keeps the RTC and backup registers alive. The family spans nine packages from 32 to 100 pins. Temperature ranges: -40 to 85 °C ambient (105 °C junction), -40 to 105 °C (125 °C junction), -40 to 125 °C (130 °C junction).
A prefetch queue and branch cache in front of the 64-bit-wide Flash; on CoreMark it gives the same performance as zero-wait-state execution from Flash at up to 80 MHz, close to 100 DMIPS.

The MPU splits memory into up to 8 protected regions, each divisible into 8 subregions, of 32 bytes up to the full 4 Gbytes. An RTOS normally drives it, reprogramming the regions per task and catching accesses to forbidden areas. It can be left off.

Up to 256 Kbytes, single bank, 128 pages of 2 Kbytes, holding code and data. Option bytes set the protections. Readout protection (RDP) has three levels: level 0, none; level 1, no Flash read or write while debug is connected or when booting from RAM or the bootloader; level 2, debug (JTAG and serial wire), boot from RAM and bootloader boot are disabled for good. Write protection (WRP) covers two areas set in 2-Kbyte steps. PCROP (proprietary code readout protection) makes an area execute-only, set in 64-bit steps: only CPU instruction fetches reach it, while DMA, debug and CPU data reads, writes and erases are blocked; the PCROP_RDP option bit chooses whether that area is erased when RDP goes from level 1 to level 0.
All non-volatile memory carries ECC: it corrects a single-bit error, detects a double-bit error, and records the failing address in the ECC register.

64 Kbytes in two blocks. SRAM1, 48 Kbytes, sits at 0x2000 0000. SRAM2, 16 Kbytes with hardware parity, sits at 0x1000 0000 and is aliased at 0x2000 C000 so that it continues SRAM1 (bit-band aliased); it is reached over the ICode/DCode buses, can be kept in Standby, and can be write-protected in 1-Kbyte steps. Both are read and written at CPU clock with no wait states.

Guards code and secure data against any access from code outside the protected areas; an illegal access resets the device at once. Three segments are set in the firewall registers: a code segment (Flash, or SRAM1 when declared executable), up to 1024 Kbytes in 256-byte steps; a non-volatile data segment in Flash, up to 1024 Kbytes in 256-byte steps; a volatile data segment in SRAM1, up to 48 Kbytes in 64-byte steps, which may be shared with unprotected code and may be executable. Entry goes through a call gate sequence. Full protection needs RDP level 2.

At start-up the BOOT0 value (from the PH3-BOOT0 pin, or from the nSWBOOT0 option bit when a user option frees the pin) and the BOOT1 option bit pick boot from user Flash, from system memory, or from embedded SRAM. If boot from main Flash is selected and the first Flash word is blank, the device boots from system memory instead. The system-memory bootloader reprograms the Flash over USART, I2C, SPI or CAN.

Computes a CRC with a configurable generator polynomial and size, for checking data transfers or storage, including Flash integrity checks under EN/IEC 60335-1 against a signature stored at link time.

VDD, 1.71 V to 3.6 V, feeds the I/Os (VDDIO1 = VDD), the internal regulator and the system analog blocks. VDDA feeds the ADC, DAC, op amp, comparators and voltage reference buffer, from 1.62 V (ADC, comparators) or 1.8 V (DAC, op amp) up to 3.6 V, independently of VDD; when none of those blocks is used, VDDA is preferably tied to VDD. VBAT, 1.55 V to 3.6 V, feeds the RTC, the 32 kHz oscillator and the backup registers through a power switch when VDD is absent. I/Os on a supply that is held at ground are not 5 V tolerant. Domains: VDDA (analog), VDD (I/O ring, reset block, temperature sensor, PLL, HSI, MSI, HSI48, standby circuitry with wakeup logic and IWDG, voltage regulator, low voltage detector), VCORE from the regulator (core, memories, digital peripherals), and the backup domain on VBAT (LSE, backup registers, RCC BDCR register, RTC).

While VDD is below 1 V, VDDA stays below VDD + 300 mV; above 1 V the supplies are independent. During power-down VDD may briefly drop below another supply only while the energy delivered to the device stays under 1 mJ, so decoupling capacitors may discharge at different rates.

An ultra-low-power brown-out reset (BOR) runs in every mode except Shutdown and holds the device in reset while VDD is below threshold, with no external reset circuit. The lowest BOR level, 1.71 V, applies at power-on; higher levels are chosen in the option bytes. A programmable voltage detector (PVD), enabled by software, compares VDD with VPVD and can interrupt when VDD falls below or rises above it. A peripheral voltage monitor (PVM) checks VDDA against a fixed threshold.

Two linear regulators feed the digital logic. The main regulator (MR) runs in Run, Sleep and Stop 0. The low-power regulator (LPR) runs in Stop 1, Stop 2, and both Low-power run and Low-power sleep, and keeps SRAM2 in Standby with SRAM2 retention. Both are off, output high impedance, in Standby and Shutdown. Dynamic voltage scaling sets VCORE: Range 1 for a CPU clock up to 80 MHz, Range 2 for up to 26 MHz with every peripheral clock also at 26 MHz or less. With the MR off and the LPR supplying VCORE the device is in Low-power run, CPU up to 2 MHz, and peripherals with their own clock can run from HSI16.

After a reset the device is in Run. Sleep stops only the CPU; peripherals keep running and an interrupt or event wakes it. Low-power run supplies VCORE from the LPR, with code in SRAM or Flash and the CPU at 2 MHz at most. Low-power sleep is entered from Low-power run, stops only the CPU clock, and returns to Low-power run on wakeup. Stop 0, 1 and 2 keep SRAM and registers, stop every VCORE clock and turn off the PLL, MSI, HSI16 and HSE, while LSE or LSI may run and the RTC may stay on; peripherals that can wake the device may turn HSI16 on to detect their wakeup event. Stop 2 puts most of VCORE into low leakage; Stop 1 has more active peripherals and wakeup sources and a shorter wakeup than Stop 2 but draws more; Stop 0 keeps the MR on for the fastest wakeup at much higher current. The clock on leaving Stop is MSI up to 48 MHz or HSI16, as software chooses.

The regulator is off, VCORE is unpowered, and the PLL, MSI, HSI16 and HSE are off; the RTC may run and the BOR stays on. Each I/O can be held with pull-up, pull-down or floating. SRAM1 and registers are lost except the backup domain and standby circuitry; SRAM2 can be kept, supplied by the LPR. Exit is by NRST, an IWDG reset, a WKUP pin edge (rising or falling, selectable), an RTC event (alarm, periodic wakeup, timestamp, tamper) or an LSE failure (CSS on LSE). On wakeup the device runs from MSI at up to 8 MHz.

The lowest-current mode: regulator off, VCORE unpowered, PLL, HSI16, MSI, LSI and HSE off; the RTC may run. There is no BOR and no supply monitoring, so switching to the backup domain is not supported. SRAM1, SRAM2 and registers are lost except the backup domain. Exit is by NRST, a WKUP pin edge (selectable) or an RTC event (alarm, periodic wakeup, timestamp, tamper). The clock after wakeup is MSI at 4 MHz.
During and after reset the I/Os are in analog state with the Schmitt trigger off, to save current, and the internal reset pull-up is turned off when the reset comes from inside.

VBAT can come from a battery, a supercapacitor, or VDD when neither is fitted; it keeps the backup registers and the LSE-clocked RTC running, and three tamper pins work in VBAT mode. The switch to VBAT is automatic when VDD goes away. A VBAT charging circuit inside can be turned on while VDD is present. Running from VBAT, external interrupts and RTC alarms or events do not end VBAT operation.

Some peripherals are wired directly to one another so they can work together without the CPU, with short and predictable latency; according to the pair, a link works in some or all of Run, Sleep, Low-power run, Low-power sleep, Stop 0, Stop 1 and Stop 2.

SYSCLK comes from one of four sources: the 4 to 48 MHz HSE crystal or ceramic resonator (or an external clock in bypass); the 16 MHz HSI16 RC, software-trimmable; the MSI RC, software-trimmable, giving 12 frequencies from 100 kHz to 48 MHz and trimmed by hardware from the LSE to better than ±0.25%; or the system PLL, fed by HSE, HSI16 or MSI, at up to 80 MHz. HSE, HSI16 and MSI can each feed a PLL. The HSI48 RC with clock recovery can clock SDMMC and RNG and can be put on MCO. For the RTC there are the 32.768 kHz LSE crystal, with four drive levels (or an external clock in bypass), and the 32 kHz LSI RC, ±5%, which also clocks the IWDG. SDMMC, RNG, SAI, USARTs, I2Cs, LPTIMs, ADC and SWPMI have independent kernel clocks; two PLLs with three outputs each can clock the ADC, SDMMC/RNG and SAI. After reset the device runs from MSI at 4 MHz. The clock security system, when enabled, moves SYSCLK to HSI16 on an HSE failure and can interrupt; an LSE failure can also be detected with an interrupt. Prescalers set AHB, APB2 (high speed) and APB1 (low speed), all at 80 MHz maximum.

MCO puts one internal clock out for external use; LSI and LSE remain available on it down to Stop 1. LSCO puts out LSI or LSE in every low-power mode down to Standby, and LSE also in Shutdown; LSCO does not work in VBAT mode.

Software makes each GPIO an output (push-pull or open-drain), an input (floating, pulled up or pulled down) or an alternate function; most share digital or analog alternate functions. The GPIOs sit on AHB2 for fast toggling. Their alternate-function setup can be locked by a set sequence against stray writes.

Two DMA controllers with 7 channels each, 14 in all, each channel tied to hardware requests and also software-triggerable. Per controller, priorities are set by software in four levels (very high, high, medium, low), with ties broken by channel number (lower first). Source and destination sizes (byte, half-word, word) are independent with packing and unpacking; addresses align to the data size. Circular buffers, transfers between any mix of memory and peripherals; Flash, SRAM, APB and AHB as source and destination; up to 65536 data per transfer. Half transfer, transfer complete and transfer error flags are ORed into one interrupt per channel.

The NVIC handles 16 priority levels and up to 67 maskable interrupt channels plus the 16 Cortex-M4 interrupt lines, with low latency, tail chaining, late-arrival handling and automatic state save and restore. The EXTI has 37 edge-detector lines that raise interrupts or events and wake the device from Stop; each line has its own rising, falling or both-edge trigger and mask, and a pending register. Internal lines come from peripherals that wake from Stop. A pulse shorter than the internal clock period is still caught. Up to 83 GPIOs map onto the 16 external interrupt lines.

One successive-approximation ADC: native 12-bit resolution, self-calibration, 5.33 Msps at 12 bits, sampling time down to 18.75 ns, faster at lower resolution (up to 8.88 Msps at 6 bits). Up to 16 external channels and 5 internal ones (VREFINT, temperature sensor, VBAT/3, DAC1_OUT1, DAC1_OUT2). An external reference pin on some packages frees the input range from the supply. Single-ended or differential inputs. Current falls in proportion to the conversion rate, and the ADC clock domain is separate from the CPU clock. Single, continuous or discontinuous sequenced scans in two groups (regular and injected), several trigger inputs from timers and pins, results to a data register or by DMA to RAM, left or right alignment, per-channel offset, hardware oversampling, per-channel sampling time, three analog watchdogs that interrupt or trigger timers, and hardware context preparation for injected channels.

Gives a voltage VTS linear in temperature, wired inside to ADC1_IN17. Its offset varies from part to part, so uncalibrated it suits only detecting changes; every device carries factory calibration values in read-only system memory (TS_CAL1 at 30 °C, TS_CAL2 at 130 °C).
VREFINT is a bandgap reference for the ADC and comparators, wired to ADC1_IN0. Its measured value, taken at 30 °C with VDDA = VREF+ = 3.0 V, is stored for each part in read-only system memory.
VBAT can be measured on ADC1_IN18 through an internal divide-by-3 bridge, since VBAT may exceed VDDA; the result is one third of VBAT.

Two buffered 12-bit DAC channels built from resistor strings and an inverting amplifier. Features: 8-bit or 12-bit mode, buffer offset calibration (factory and user), left or right alignment in 12-bit mode, synchronized update, noise and triangle wave generation, independent or simultaneous dual conversion, DMA per channel, external triggers, and a low-power sample-and-hold mode with an internal or external capacitor. Timer update outputs, also routed to DMA channels, trigger the DAC.

VREFBUF drives VREF+ at 2.048 V or 2.5 V as the reference for the ADC, DAC and outside parts. With the buffer off, an external reference goes on VREF+. A 100 nF capacitor on VREF+ sets the low-frequency cut-off. On packages where VREF+ is bonded to VDDA the buffer is not available.

Two comparators, rail-to-rail, with selectable reference, hysteresis, speed (a low-speed, low-power setting) and output polarity. The reference is an I/O, a DAC output, or VREFINT or 1/4, 1/2 or 3/4 of it. Both wake the device from Stop, raise interrupts and timer breaks, and can be paired as a window comparator.
One op amp with external or internal follower routing and a programmable-gain (PGA) mode; low input bias current, low offset, a low-power mode and rail-to-rail input.

Senses capacitance by surface charge transfer to detect a finger near an electrode behind a dielectric such as glass or plastic. Up to 21 channels, up to 3 acquired in parallel, one sampling capacitor per group of up to 3 channels, spread spectrum against noise, full hardware acquisition sequence, programmable charge transfer frequency, sampling-capacitor and channel pins, a max count limit for a faulty channel, flags for acquisition end and for max count error, each able to interrupt. Suits proximity, touchkey, linear and rotary sensors, with the STMTouch library. The channel count depends on the package and free I/Os.
Delivers 32-bit random numbers from an analog circuit on the chip.

Timer set: TIM1 (advanced control); general-purpose TIM2, TIM15 and TIM16; basic TIM6 and TIM7; LPTIM1 and LPTIM2; IWDG and WWDG; SysTick. TIM1 is a three-phase PWM over 6 channels with complementary outputs and programmable dead time; its 4 channels do input capture, output compare, edge- or center-aligned PWM from 0 to 100%, and one-pulse output. In debug its counter can freeze and its PWM outputs shut off. It links with the TIMx timers for synchronization or chaining.

TIM2 has a 32-bit auto-reload up/down counter and 32-bit prescaler, 4 channels for capture, compare, PWM or one-pulse, quadrature encoder support and its own DMA requests. TIM15 (2 channels, 1 complementary) and TIM16 (1 channel, 1 complementary) have 16-bit auto-reload up counters and 16-bit prescalers, and every channel does capture, compare, PWM or one-pulse. All link for synchronization or chaining, have their own DMA requests, and freeze in debug. TIM6 and TIM7 are 16-bit time bases, mostly for triggering the DAC.

LPTIM1 and LPTIM2 have their own clock and keep running in Stop when clocked from LSE, LSI or an external clock, and they wake the device from Stop. LPTIM1 runs in Stop 0, 1 and 2; LPTIM2 in Stop 0 and 1. Each has a 16-bit up counter with 16-bit autoreload and a 16-bit compare register, pulse or PWM output, continuous or one-shot mode, software or hardware trigger, a clock from LSE, LSI, HSI16, APB or an external input (counting pulses even with no internal clock running), a digital glitch filter, and encoder mode on LPTIM1 only.
IRTIM drives an infrared LED for remote control on IR_OUT, building its waveform from TIM15 and TIM16 output channels.

The IWDG is a 12-bit down counter with an 8-bit prescaler on the 32 kHz LSI, independent of the main clock, so it runs in Stop and Standby; it resets the device or serves as a free-running timeout, is started by hardware or software per the option bytes, and freezes in debug. The WWDG is a 7-bit down counter on the main clock with an early warning interrupt, freezing in debug. SysTick is a 24-bit down counter with autoreload, a maskable interrupt at zero and a programmable clock, meant for an RTOS.

The RTC counts in BCD on its own clock: calendar with subseconds, seconds, minutes, hours (12 or 24 h), weekday, date, month and year; automatic month length and leap year; two alarms; on-the-fly correction of 1 to 32767 RTC clock pulses; reference clock detection on a 50 or 60 Hz source; digital calibration with 0.95 ppm resolution; three tamper pins with programmable filter; timestamp on a pin event, a tamper event or a switch to VBAT; and a 17-bit auto-reload wakeup timer. The RTC and 32 backup registers (128 bytes) are fed from VDD when present, otherwise from VBAT; the registers survive system and power resets and wakeup from Standby or Shutdown. RTC clock: 32.768 kHz LSE crystal, external resonator or oscillator on LSE, LSI (32 kHz typical) or HSE/32. On LSE the RTC works in VBAT mode and every low-power mode; on LSI it works in every low-power mode except Shutdown and not in VBAT mode. Every RTC event can interrupt and wake the device.

Three I2C interfaces compatible with I2C-bus specification rev. 5: master and slave, multimaster, Standard-mode to 100 kbit/s, Fast-mode to 400 kbit/s, Fast-mode Plus to 1 Mbit/s with 20 mA output drive, 7- and 10-bit addressing with several 7-bit slave addresses, programmable setup and hold, optional clock stretching. SMBus 2.0 with hardware PEC, ARP and alert; PMBus 1.1. An independent kernel clock keeps the bus speed fixed when PCLK changes. Wakeup from Stop on address match, analog and digital noise filters, a 1-byte buffer with DMA.

USART1, USART2 and USART3: asynchronous, IrDA SIR ENDEC, multiprocessor, single-wire half-duplex, LIN master/slave, hardware CTS/RTS, RS485 driver enable, up to 10 Mbit/s; also smartcard (ISO 7816) and SPI-like synchronous mode. Their clock domain is separate from the CPU, so they wake the device from Stop at up to 204 kbaud on a start bit, any received frame or a given frame. All are served by DMA.

One low-power UART: asynchronous, half-duplex single wire, CTS/RTS, multiprocessor. With its own clock domain it wakes the device from Stop at up to 220 kbaud, on a start bit, any received frame or a given frame. The 32.768 kHz LSE alone allows 9600 baud, so it can wait for a frame in Stop at very low current; a faster clock gives higher rates. Served by DMA.

Three SPIs, up to 40 Mbit/s as master and 24 Mbit/s as slave, half-duplex, full-duplex or simplex. A 3-bit prescaler gives 8 master frequencies; frames are 4 to 16 bits. Supports TI mode, NSS pulse mode and CRC in hardware. Served by DMA.

One serial audio interface with two independent sub-blocks, each transmitter or receiver with an 8-word FIFO, synchronous or asynchronous to each other, each master or slave, each with its own clock generator in master mode. Data of 8, 10, 16, 20, 24 or 32 bits; protocols including I2S, PCM/DSP, TDM, AC'97, SPDIF output, and MSB- or LSB-justified; 16 slots at most of configurable size with selectable active slots; configurable bits per frame, frame sync level, offset and length, first bit position, LSB or MSB first; mute; stereo or mono; selectable SCK strobing edge. Error flags (overrun, underrun, early or late frame sync in slave mode, codec not ready in AC'97 receive) and FIFO requests can interrupt; two DMA channels serve the FIFOs.

Single wire protocol master interface for a contactless front end per ETSI TS 102 613: full duplex, automatic bus state handling (active, suspend, resume), bit rate up to 2 Mbit/s, hardware handling of SOF, EOF and CRC. Served by DMA.

bxCAN to 2.0A and 2.0B active at up to 1 Mbit/s, standard 11-bit and extended 29-bit identifiers. Three transmit mailboxes with configurable priority, two 3-stage receive FIFOs with configurable overrun, 14 scalable filter banks with identifier lists. Time-triggered option: no automatic retransmission, a 16-bit free-running timer, timestamp in the last two data bytes. Maskable interrupts; mailboxes in one address space.

Card host interface between APB and MultiMediaCards, SD memory and SDIO cards: MMC System Specification 4.2 with 1-, 4- and 8-bit buses and older MMC versions, SD memory 2.0, SD I/O 2.0 with 1- and 4-bit buses, up to 48 MHz in 8-bit mode, DMA.

CRS trims the internal 48 MHz oscillator automatically across the operating range from a sync signal: the LSE, an external signal on CRS_SYNC, or software. Manual trimming can be combined with it for faster lock at start-up.

Interface to single, dual or quad SPI Flash in indirect, status-polling or memory-mapped mode; dual-flash mode reads two memories at once, 8 bits at a time, doubling throughput and capacity. SDR and DDR; programmable opcode and frame format; instruction, address, alternate-byte, dummy and data phases each configurable; FIFO for receive and transmit; 8-, 16- and 32-bit accesses; DMA in indirect mode; flag masking, timeout, and interrupts on FIFO threshold, timeout, status match, completion and access error.

The SWJ-DP combines JTAG and serial wire debug. Serial wire needs 2 pins instead of the 5 of JTAG: SWDIO shares JTMS and SWCLK shares JTCK, and a sequence on TMS switches between JTAG-DP and SW-DP; unused JTAG pins can be GPIOs. The Embedded Trace Macrocell streams compressed instruction and data trace over a few ETM pins to an external trace port analyzer.

Unless a note says otherwise, every I/O is an analog input during and after reset. PA13, PA14, PA15, PB3 and PB4 come out of reset as JTAG/SW debug pins, with pull-ups on PA15, PA13 and PB4 and a pull-down on PA14. PC13, PC14 and PC15 are fed through the power switch, which sinks only 3 mA, so as outputs they are limited to 2 MHz into 30 pF and must not source current; after a Backup domain power-up their function follows the RTC registers. On the UFQFPN32, PA0 also carries CK_IN.

The 4-Gbyte space is split into eight 512-Mbyte blocks: code (Flash, system memory, aliased boot memory) from 0x0000 0000, SRAM from 0x2000 0000, peripherals from 0x4000 0000, the QUADSPI Flash bank at 0x9000 0000, QUADSPI registers at 0xA000 1000, and the Cortex-M4 internal peripherals from 0xE000 0000. Addresses 0x0000 0000 to 0x0003 FFFF show Flash, system memory or SRAM according to the boot setting.

Voltages are referred to VSS. Min and max figures hold over the worst case of temperature, supply and clock and are tested on every part at TA = 25 °C and at the top of its temperature range; figures marked as characterization or design are not tested in production, and characterization limits are the mean ±3σ. Typical figures are at TA = 25 °C, VDD = VDDA = 3 V, for guidance only. Typical ADC accuracy is the error that 95 % of a sample batch stays within over temperature (mean ±2σ). Curves are guidance and are not tested. Pins are loaded with 50 pF when measured.

Each supply pair is decoupled with ceramic capacitors as close to the pins as possible, or under them on the back of the board: 100 nF at every VDD pin plus one 4.7 µF, 10 nF plus 1 µF at VDDA, and 100 nF plus 1 µF at VREF+. The 10 nF part at VDDA is a good ceramic close to the chip. VBAT takes 1.55 V to 3.6 V and powers the LSE, the RTC and the backup registers through the power switch.
IDD_ALL in the supply current tables is the whole part's draw: VDD, VDDA and VBAT together.
Past the absolute maximum ratings the part can be damaged; they are stress limits, the part is not meant to run at them, and long exposure can cut its life. The mission profile follows JEDEC JESD47.

Supply currents are taken with every I/O in analog input mode, every peripheral off unless named, the fewest Flash wait states for fHCLK (RM0394), and fPCLK = fHCLK whenever peripherals run. Current depends on supply, temperature, pin loads, software setup, clock rates, pin toggling, the memory the code runs from and the code itself.

An input with pull-up draws current, set by the pull resistor, while something outside holds it low; an output also feeds any outside pull-down or load. An input held at a mid-level voltage draws current through its Schmitt trigger; analog mode avoids this, and ADC inputs belong in analog mode. A floating input can drift to mid-level or toggle from noise, so unused pins go to analog mode or to a fixed level (pull resistor or output mode). A toggling pin also draws the current that charges its load capacitance (ISW).

Each figure in the peripheral current table is the change in supply current between the peripheral clocked and not clocked, with every I/O in analog mode; it covers the digital part only. The analog parts' currents are given with each analog block.
Wakeup times run from the wakeup event to the first user instruction; the part enters the low-power mode with a WFE instruction.
In bypass mode the HSE (or LSE) oscillator is off and OSC_IN (or OSC32_IN) is a plain GPIO input that must meet the I/O characteristics; the clock shape is defined by high and low levels and times.

The HSE runs from a 4 MHz to 48 MHz crystal or ceramic resonator. Its figures come from design simulation with typical external parts. Resonator and load capacitors sit as close to the oscillator pins as possible to keep distortion and start-up time down. ST application note AN2867 covers crystal choice.

The LSE runs from a 32.768 kHz crystal; its figures come from design simulation with typical external parts. Crystal and load capacitors sit as close to the pins as possible. No resistor may be fitted between OSC32_IN and OSC32_OUT. The drive strength (LSEDRV[1:0]) sets the current and the largest crystal gm the oscillator can start.
The internal clock figures are taken under the general operating conditions; their curves come from characterization and are not tested in production.

Susceptibility is checked on samples during characterization, with a simple program toggling two LEDs: ESD is applied to every pin (IEC 61000-4-2) and fast transient bursts to VDD and VSS through 100 pF (IEC 61000-4-4) until the LEDs show a fault; a reset brings the part back. Results depend heavily on the application software, which should handle a corrupted program counter, an unexpected reset and corrupted control registers. Most faults can be provoked by holding NRST or the oscillator pins low for 1 s, and ESD can be applied to the part directly to test the software's recovery (AN1015). Emission is measured per IEC 61967-2.

ESD stress is a positive then a negative pulse 1 s apart on every pin combination, on 3 parts × (n + 1) supply pins, per ANSI/JEDEC. Latch-up is tested on six parts with overvoltage on each supply pin and current injection on each I/O pin, per EIA/JESD 78A.

Driving pins below VSS or above VDDIOx should be avoided in normal use. Injection robustness is checked on samples with pins in floating input mode, one at a time; a fault is an ADC error over 5 LSB TUE, leakage on neighbouring pins outside -5 µA to +0 µA, a reset or an oscillator frequency shift. Negative injection causes negative induced leakage and positive injection positive leakage.
The I/Os are designed to be CMOS- and TTL-compliant.

A GPIO sinks or sources up to ±8 mA at the rated levels and up to ±20 mA with relaxed VOL/VOH. The current all I/Os source plus the MCU's own draw on VDD stays under ΣIVDD; the current all I/Os sink plus the MCU's own draw on VSS stays under ΣIVSS.
The maximum frequency is reached when tr + tf ≤ 2/3 of the period and the duty cycle is 45 % to 55 % into the rated load.
NRST is a CMOS input with a permanent pull-up RPU. An outside capacitor on it guards against stray resets and goes as close to the part as possible.
A pulse on an interrupt input has to last at least 20 ns for the event controller to catch it.

Run a calibration after every power-up. Below VDDA = 2.4 V the analog switch booster is enabled (BOOSTEN in SYSCFG_CFGR1). The fast channels are PC0 to PC3, PA0 and PA1; the rest are slow. Negative current into one analog pin spoils conversions on others, so a Schottky diode to ground on pins that may see it is advised. Board capacitance on an input costs accuracy; lowering fADC recovers it. Decouple as the power supply scheme shows, with the 10 nF ceramic close to the chip.
The DAC has an output buffer that lowers its output impedance so it can drive loads without an outside op-amp; BOFFx in DAC_CR bypasses it.
The timer figures are set by design; their pins follow the I/O port characteristics.

The I2C meets the I2C-bus specification (rev. 03) timing for Standard-mode (100 kbit/s), Fast-mode (400 kbit/s) and Fast-mode Plus (1 Mbit/s), by design, when configured as RM0394 describes. SDA and SCL are not true open-drain: in open-drain mode the PMOS to VDDIOx is off but still there. Only FT_f pins meet the Fm+ sink current. Every SDA and SCL pin has an analog spike filter.

SPI, Quad SPI, SAI and SD/MMC timings are taken under the general operating conditions with the pin speed at OSPEEDRy[1:0] = 11 (10 for the SAI), a 30 pF load (15 or 20 pF for Quad SPI) and edges measured at 0.5 × VDD; the points in the SPI timing diagrams are at 0.3 VDD and 0.7 VDD.
The CAN_TX and CAN_RX pins follow the I/O port characteristics.
The SWPMI and its SWPMI_IO transceiver meet ETSI TS 102 613.

Nine packages: LQFP100 (14 x 14 mm), UFBGA100 (7 x 7 mm), LQFP64 (10 x 10 mm), UFBGA64 (5 x 5 mm), WLCSP64 (3.141 x 3.127 mm, 0.35 mm pitch), WLCSP49 (3.141 x 3.127 mm, 0.4 mm pitch), LQFP48 (7 x 7 mm), UFQFPN48 (7 x 7 mm) and UFQFPN32 (5 x 5 mm). All but the WLCSPs have a 0.5 mm pitch. Both UFQFPN packages carry an exposed pad underneath that goes to board ground.

The top face carries the product identification, a date code (year digit, two-digit week), a revision code and a pin 1 or ball A1 mark; extra marks used through the supply chain may also appear. Engineering samples, marked ES or E or shipped with a notice saying so, are not qualified for production use.

Each temperature suffix sets an ambient guaranteed at full dissipation and a junction limit. Few designs run at full dissipation, so the actual power and junction temperature are worked out with the package's ΘJA and the suffix chosen from that. For LQFP64 the allowed dissipation falls linearly from about 650 mW to zero between 75 °C and 105 °C ambient for suffix 6, and between 95 °C and 125 °C for suffix 7.
